card.title: Liquid State: Physical Properties of Liquids

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: A liquid is a tug-of-war frozen mid-pull: molecules touch but keep trading partners. **Evaporation** lets the fastest surface molecules escape at any temperature — and their departure is why sweat cools. In a closed flask, escape and return balance into **dynamic equilibrium**, and the vapour's steady pressure is a property of liquid-plus-temperature alone.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text: - Boiling condition: vapour pressure = external pressure - Water VP: 23.8 mmHg at 25 °C - Surface tension of water: 0.072 N/m (25 °C) - Viscosity of water: ≈ 1 cP (20 °C)

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **Boiling vs evaporation:** boiling is bulk-wide, at a fixed T set by external pressure; evaporation is surface-only, at any T — the comparison table is the answer frame.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: "A liquid boils when its vapour pressure becomes equal to the external pressure."

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***The sweating athlete*** — evaporation of sweat removes the fastest water molecules, carrying away ~2.4 kJ per gram — the body's radiator.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Covers only: liquid state, physical properties of liquids — evaporation, condensation, vapour pressure (within States of Matter).  ·  Out of scope here: topics of neighbouring units in Chemistry — don't mix them.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — The In-Between State Liquids hold a shapeless volume: molecules touch but keep trading places. Four measurable properties — vapour pressure, boiling point, surface tension, viscosity — all trace back to the same balance of attraction and thermal motion, and each one has a favourite exam question.  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts ### 2.1 Evaporation and condensation - **Evaporation:** surface molecules with above-average kinetic energy escape the liquid; it occurs at **all temperatures**, faster with higher T, larger surface, lower humidity and air movement. - **Condensation:** the reverse — vapour molecules return to the liquid.…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: BP rule: "external P up → BP up". γ and η both fall with T; VP rises. Viscosity champions: glycerine, honey, H₂SO₄. Surface tension champion: Hg > H₂O.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: **NEB-style (2m): Define vapour pressure of a liquid. Why is it independent of the amount of liquid taken?** — The **vapour pressure** of a liquid is the pressure exerted by its vapour when in dynamic equilibrium with the liquid in a closed container: molecules evaporate from the surface at the same rate as vapour molecules condense…  ·  **NEB-style (2m): Water boils at about 70 °C on Mount Everest but at about 120 °C inside a pressure cooker. Explain.** — A liquid **boils when its vapour pressure equals the external pressure**.…

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: For boiling-point-at-altitude answers, write the defining equality (VP = external P) first, then apply it to the two pressures — the definition earns the mark, the application earns the rest.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: All four properties are read-outs of the same molecular tug-of-war: intermolecular attraction (holding molecules together) versus thermal energy (pulling them apart). Heat shifts every property in the same direction — VP up, BP up, γ down, η down.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Evaporation: surface escape at all T; cools the liquid (high-energy molecules leave). Vapour pressure: dynamic equilibrium in closed vessel; depends only on liquid + T. Boiling: VP = external pressure; 100 °C at 1 atm, ~70 °C on Everest, ~120 °C at 2 atm.…

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Mercury's enormous surface tension (0.48 N/m) and high viscosity-consistency make it convex-meniscused and non-wetting — the reason old thermometers read cleanly.

rows.text: **NEB-style (2m): Why does evaporation cause cooling of the remaining liquid?** — Molecules in a liquid share a distribution of kinetic energies. **Evaporation is selective:** only the fastest, highest-energy molecules at the surface escape.…

Common Confusions **Vapour pressure exists below the boiling point too:** every liquid in a closed flask has a vapour pressure at room temperature; boiling merely marks where it equals the atmosphere.  ·  **Viscosity and surface tension are different properties:** viscosity resists *flow* (bulk), surface tension resists *area increase* (surface) — glycerine is viscous, mercury has huge surface tension; the two don't track each other.
